# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

...

Lambda has done the renter-friendly thing — announced, dated and quantified, ten days ahead — and the size is the story: about 15% at once, on the three cards that anchor most training budgets. Anyone renewing or reserving Lambda capacity this month now has a hard date to plan around, and Nov 16 becomes a date this desk will verify first thing.

# Verda raises prices for the tenth time — eight GPUs up about 1%, the L40S holds

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 5: eight of Verda's nine tracked GPUs rose by about 1% — the tenth rise since Oct 23. The L40S held, the first card Verda has left flat on a rise day in this run. The same morning, Lambda announced rises of about 15% for Nov 16.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on verda.com/pricing

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 6, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.31 → $13.44 [$13.44], B300 $11.57 → $11.69 [$11.69], B200 $9.05 → $9.14 [$9.138], H200 $6.38 → $6.44 [$6.440], H100 SXM $4.89 → $4.94 [$4.938], A100 80GB $2.29 → $2.32 [$2.316], A100 40GB $1.64 → $1.66 [$1.657] and RTX PRO 6000 $2.70 → $2.73 [$2.725]. The L40S held at $1.94 [$1.939]. Each rise is within a whisker of +1.0% — the same uniform list adjustment as the nine before it.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, held Oct 31 and Nov 1, rose an eighth time on Nov 2, held Nov 3, rose a ninth time on Nov 4, held Nov 5 — and has now risen a tenth time. Its GB300, the only GB300 rate we list, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.44 today, up 13.7% in eighteen days. And Verda is no longer the pattern's only mover: Nebius raised across the board on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, SaladCloud's Priority rise took effect Nov 1, RunPod Serverless rose by Nov 2, and Lambda today announced rises of about 15% effective Nov 16. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $66 per B200 and $36 per H100 on a 730-hour month.

Checked today and unchanged: RunPod Secure, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, TensorDock and SaladCloud all held at the rates read on Nov 5. Not checked today, and named rather than covered by the stamp: Hyperstack (its pricing table could not be read, for the ninth straight day), Lambda's currently-effective rates (now visible only after logging in; its announced Nov 16 rates are reported separately today), RunPod Community (its tier could not be separated in today's read) and nafnaf.ai (its homepage showed no GPUs available today).

...

Ten rises in fifteen days, and now a second provider announcing a rise five times larger in a single step: the autumn pattern has widened from one provider's steady repricing into something broader. The renter's spread is still the story — a workload priced off Verda's list page in mid-October is nearly 14% adrift on the GB300 today, while the cheapest verified way to rent most cards has not moved at all. Check the board before renewing at a list rate — and if you are on Verda's GB300 or A100 40GB, your best-offer price moved today.

results.title: AWS Raises GPU Prices 15% as Cloud Backlog Hits $2.48T | TechSignal.news
highlights:
TechSignal.news AI November 6, 2026 4 min read

## AWS reprices GPU capacity for the third time in 2026

AWS raised prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by approximately 15% on October 7 for most U.S. GPU configurations. The increase follows a 15% rise on January 4, a 10% increase in April for selected configurations, and a 20% jump on July 1. Reserved GPU capacity—once positioned as a hedge against spot-market volatility—now exhibits its own price instability.

The repricing reflects demand conditions AWS cannot suppress through incremental capacity additions. Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon and Alphabet disclosed combined cloud backlogs of approximately $2.48 trillion in their latest results: Microsoft $677 billion, Oracle $664 billion, Amazon $578 billion, and Google $561 billion. These commitments represent contracted future revenue, not available infrastructure. For enterprise buyers, the gap between committed spend and deployable capacity creates procurement risk.

# Platts to launch US GPU Compute Prices, Nov. 23

Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, will launch US GPU Compute prices, effective Nov. 23, 2026.

Daily on-demand and interruptible prices will cover four NVIDIA chips: the NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and B300 chips. Prices will be published in US dollars per GPU-hour and US dollars per million tokens of output, based on prices and availability at 1:30 pm CT.

COVERAGE

The assessments reflect the market value of available NVIDIA GPU compute capacity delivered through qualifying virtualized infrastructure services in the US by providers and marketplaces. The new assessments will capture an evolving segment of the compute market, where growing availability of dedicated GPU capacity and increasingly standardized service offerings have supported greater price transparency. The assessments will provide standardized price references for accessing GPU compute capacity in the US, adding further granularity to Platts coverage of the infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence workloads.

METHODOLOGY

Each GPU price will be a simple average of the prices of available GPUs for each chip and service type. Platts will review the prices for outliers and will automatically exclude any prices greater than 2 median absolute deviations from the median.

Platts may review the suitability of the current methodology and consider adopting a volume-weighted average approach once sufficient trade data has been collected. Platts encourages market participants to report trade data to ComputePricing@spglobal.com (PriceGroup@spglobal.com) for this purpose.

results.title: Cloud GPU Pricing 2026: H100, B200 and RTX Rental Costs
results.author: Boris Sedu
highlights:
- An H100 costs about $2–12 per GPU-hour on demand depending on the provider: around $2 on marketplaces, $4–6 on AI-focused clouds such as Lambda, RunPod, Nebius and CoreWeave, and $7–12 on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Oracle.
- Newer GPUs cost more per hour but not always per job. A B200 rents for about $6.70–8.50 on AI clouds, but it trains roughly twice as fast as an H100, so the total cost of a job can be the same or lower.
- Consumer and mid-range GPUs are cheap: an RTX 4090 or RTX 5090 rents for roughly $0.30–1.20 per hour, an A100 80GB for $0.70–3.50.
- Prices rose in 2026. Nebius raised on-demand prices by about 17–21% on October 1, AWS raised Capacity Block prices three times, and several clouds moved the H100 from $2.99 to $3.99 per hour.
- Newer GPUs and better software change the math. In MLPerf Training 2026, NVIDIA’s GB300 was 1.3–1.6 times faster than the GB200, and the independent ClusterMAX rating put CoreWeave and Nebius at the top for cluster quality.
- Spot and reserved capacity cut costs by roughly 30–80%, but spot instances can be interrupted at any moment, and reservations lock you in.

...

- Nebius raised on-demand prices on October 1, 2026: H100 from $3.85 to $4.50 per hour, H200 from $4.50 to $5.40, B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.
- AWS raised prices of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, its reserved GPU capacity, by about 15% in January 2026, by about 20% in July (P5 with H100 to $5.19 per GPU-hour, P6-B200 to $12.36) and again in October.
- RunPod and Lambda list the H100 SXM at $3.99 per hour; in spring 2026 both were quoted at $2.99 or less. RunPod’s B200 rose from about $5.89 to $7.99.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Oct 2026: Vast.ai Swings, Verda +15-21% | TransAtlas
results.author: TransAtlas Editorial
highlights:
GPU Cloud Pricing Oct 2026: Vast.ai Swings, Verda +15-21% | TransAtlas

# GPU Cloud Pricing Oct 2026: Vast.ai Swings, Verda +15-21%

On-demand floor-price month-over-month from two snapshots (Sep 23 vs Oct 15 2026): AWS/OCI/Lambda flat, Vast.ai swinging more than 100%, Verda matched models up 15–21%, with new models and a price cheat-sheet.

 TransAtlas Editorial · November 5, 2026 · 5 min Copy link 

 On this page 9

- Key takeaways (30-second read)
- 1. Methodology and Comparable Window
- 2. Platform Trend: Who Moved, Who Did Not
- 3. Biggest Movers (on-demand floor, month-over-month)
- 4. Newly Listed Models (added in the Oct 2026 snapshot)
- 5. End-of-Period Lowest Price Cheat-Sheet (Oct 15, 2026 snapshot, ex-GCP)
- 6. Buying Advice
- Sources
- FAQ

## Key takeaways (30-second read)

> Hyperscalers and Lambda Labs barely moved in October: the median on-demand floor price across matched models was flat (0%). The action was on two specialized clouds: Vast.ai (a P2P marketplace) had a median +12.3% swing, range -67% to +153%, while Verda's matched models rose +15% to +21%. Biggest single-card jump: Vast.ai RTX 6000 Ada from $0.22 to $0.57 (+153%); biggest drop: Vast.ai RTX PRO 4500 from $1.04 to $0.35 (-67%). New listings clustered on Verda (added 10 models in October including B200/B300/GB300/H200) and Vast.ai (added 8 including A100/H100 NVL). About GCP on-demand: the absolute figures in these snapshots predate our 2026-10-31 switch to Google's official billing catalog, so this report does not quote GCP on-demand absolutes: only relative movement. Authoritative GCP numbers are in AWS vs Azure vs GCP.

## 1. Methodology and Comparable Window

All GPU cloud pricing figures come from two TransAtlas price-database snapshots, expressed as USD per single GPU per hour, lowest on-demand listed price:

- Start: 2026-09-23 (1,626 listings covering aws/azure/gcp/lambdalabs/oci/vastai/verda/vultr, among others)
- End: 2026-10-15 (1,345 listings covering the same eight providers)

All eight providers appear in both snapshots, but only seven have overlapping (matched) models for the month-over-month pairing: Vultr's models do not overlap across the two periods, so it appears only as a new listing in §4. For each matched card we pair the lowest on-demand listed price on each platform. Caliber details:

- On-demand quotes only (both dedicated and marketplace); Spot is excluded from the main tables.
- Per-GPU quotes only; the pre-normalization whole-instance price and GPU count stay available so anyone can recompute.
- The start snapshot did not capture live availability, so its floor may include a few currently-unrentable listings; that is fine for "floor-price direction" and does not change the sign of movement.
- GCP on-demand absolutes in both snapshots predate the official-source correction, so we quote no GCP absolutes here, only relative movement.

...

The table below shows each platform's median on-demand floor-price movement across matched models. 0% does not mean the price is zero: it means every matched model's two endpoints were essentially unchanged.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | 7 | 0.0% | 0.0% ~ 0.0% |
| Azure | 5 | 0.0% | -34.8% ~ 0.0% |
| GCP | 11 | 0.0%* | 0.0% ~ 0.0% |
| Lambda Labs | 5 | 0.0% | 0.0% ~ 0.0% |
| OCI | 3 | 0.0% | 0.0% ~ 0.0% |
| Vast.ai | 8 | +12.3% | -66.6% ~ +153.4% |
| Verda | 3 | +17.0% | +15.1% ~ +20.7% |

* GCP marked with an asterisk means its absolutes are not official-source corrected; read it as relative only. The takeaway is clear: hyperscaler prices (AWS/OCI/Lambda) are highly sticky; the volatility lives in market-priced specialized clouds.

results.title: Setara Joins GPU Price Race Behind Ornn's $3.38/hr [2026]
results.author: Chloe Bennett
highlights:
Setara Financial Corp. announced on November 3, 2026 that it has released the Setara Index, its first daily benchmark for on-demand graphics processing unit rental prices. The index, unveiled in Chicago, tracks seven GPU models and expresses pricing in U.S. dollars per GPU-hour, updated every day using what the company calls its proprietary Benchmark Creation Engine. It lands at a moment when GPU capacity has become one of the most contested and least transparent commodities in the global economy, and when at least two other firms are already racing to own the reference price for AI compute.

...

The mechanics are straightforward on paper. The index draws on publicly available on-demand list prices published by independent GPU providers, covering seven GPU models, and converts that into a single daily reference figure per GPU-hour. Setara has not published the identities of the seven models or the specific providers it pulls from, so outside observers cannot yet replicate or audit the exact inputs. The index itself is hosted on Setara’s dedicated GPU Index page, separate from the company’s main site.

...

Provider-level pricing tells a similar story of upward pressure. RunPod, one of the larger GPU rental marketplaces, raised its Secure Cloud and Instant Cluster rates twice in the span of about a month heading into November, with its own pricing changelog tracked by UsagePricing’s pricing-change monitor showing a second hike in mid-October after an earlier increase in September. SemiAnalysis’s longer-run composite tells the other side of the cycle: its H100 index fell from roughly $6.62 per GPU-hour in the second half of 2023 to about $2.83 by February 2026, even as 1-year contract prices for the same chip climbed back from a late-2024 trough near $1.70 toward $2.65.
